newsitem.title: USA: ING chair wants to up U.S. shr percentage.
newsitem.headline: ING chair wants to up U.S. shr percentage.

text.p: ING Groep N.V. chairman Aad Jacobs said Friday he would like to double the percentage of the company's shares held by U.S. investors.

Speaking shortly after American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) for the Dutch financial services group began trading on the New York Stock Exchange, Jacobs said he would be "very pleased" if the level held by U.S. investors rose to 25 percent.
They now hold about 13 percent. Asked what percentage he would like to see, he said, "That is a difficult question, but let me say that at least we can double (the percentage of shares held) here."
He added, "At least 22 percent of our earnings are coming from this continent, so that would be the minimum. But if I can get 25 percent, I would be very pleased."
He denied that the recent purchase of 500,000 shares of Portugal's Banco Mello represented a takeover bid and called it a "token of friendship."
ING has substantial insurance operations, and Jacobs described Portugal's insurance market as "a very interesting one. Economically, Portugal is doing extremely well."

Asked if ING, the Netherlands' second-largest bank, had takeover plans for Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd, Jacobs said, "I can tell you that that is a rumor I have read in the newspaper also."
Queried if there was any truth to the rumor, he said, "Absolutely not."
ING ADRs were priced to open at $46.483. They began trading at 46-3/4 and in early afternoon had eased slightly to 46-1/2.
The bank was offering 6.5 million ADRs with a one-to-one ratio to underlying shares.
Jacobs said reasons for trading in New York included making it easier for U.S. investors to trade in the stock and having more shares available for possible acquisitions in the United States.

ING's acquisition talks with Oppenheimer & Co fell apart. ING also broke off talks with Wall Street investment bank Dillon Read & Co, recently bought by Swiss Bank Corp to buy the 75 percent of the firm it did not already own.
Jacobs said ING was still "very much interested" in buying a U.S. investment bank but said prices were "at the top."
"We are not in a hurry, but we are looking around," he said.
He said ING was willing to spend "more than a couple billion dollars" for the purchase of a U.S. insurance company.
